title: Quiet in the third hour
note: Fictional child. Values are illustrative; your unit’s pediatric protocol and the pediatric nephrologist’s orders come first.
intro: Jasmine Ortiz, 11 years old and 30 kilograms, is on hemodialysis through a tunneled catheter. Today’s order is to remove 1,200 mL over 3 hours, about 13.3 mL/kg/h. She is near her target weight. Her baseline heart rate is about 90. Her mother is reading in the chair beside her.

vitals.child: Quiet, yawning, asks to lie flat

n1.scene: Jasmine stops playing, yawns again and again, and asks to lie flat. Her heart rate has risen to 108. Her blood pressure is still in her usual range. Her mother says she is just tired.

choices.text: Go to her now: lay her flat, recheck blood pressure and heart rate, reduce or pause fluid removal per protocol, and tell the nephrologist.
choices.feedback: Yawning, quietness and a rising heart rate are early signs of falling blood volume in a child. Blood pressure is a late sign. Acting now prevents a crash.

choices.text: Note it and recheck in 30 minutes, since her blood pressure is normal.
choices.feedback: A normal blood pressure is reassuring in an adult, not in a child. Compensation hides the problem until it fails.
choices.then: Ten minutes later she looks pale. You lay her flat and pause fluid removal.

choices.text: Increase fluid removal slightly so she still reaches her target on time.
choices.feedback: Faster removal in a child who is already showing intolerance pushes her toward collapse. A rate she does not tolerate is too fast, whatever the number says.
choices.then: Within minutes she becomes pale and sweaty. You lay her flat and pause fluid removal.

n2.scene: Fluid removal is paused. Jasmine is flat, but her hands are cool and her capillary refill is 3 seconds. Her heart rate is 112.

choices.text: Call the nephrologist now with SBAR, keep fluid removal off, and check vital signs every 5 minutes while you wait for orders.
choices.feedback: She is still compensating, but she has not recovered with simple measures. The prescriber decides on fluid and on the rest of the session.

choices.text: Give a saline bolus from the line on your own.
choices.feedback: Fluid may well be what she needs, but it is given as ordered or under your unit’s standing protocol, not by guess. Call first.
choices.then: You call the nephrologist, who gives an order for fluid per protocol.

choices.text: Restart fluid removal at the original rate, since her blood pressure is still above 90.
choices.feedback: A single number above a line is not safety. Her heart rate, color and refill say she is not ready.
choices.then: Her pressure drops within minutes. You stop removal and call the nephrologist.

n3.scene: After fluid given as ordered, Jasmine looks better: color back, heart rate 98. About 300 mL of the planned removal is left, with 20 minutes to go.
n3.prompt: How do you handle the rest of the session?

choices.text: Follow the nephrologist’s revised goal, even if she ends above her target weight, and watch her closely to the end.
choices.feedback: Chasing the target in a child who just showed intolerance risks a second episode. The target weight itself may need review.

choices.text: Extend the session and remove the remaining 300 mL at a faster rate.
choices.feedback: Faster removal after an episode is how a second, worse episode happens. The goal is the nephrologist’s to change.
choices.then: The nephrologist revises the goal; you continue gently.

choices.text: End the session now without asking.
choices.feedback: Caution is reasonable, but ending treatment is a prescriber decision, and she may still need clearance.
choices.then: You check with the nephrologist, who sets a revised goal.

n4.scene: The blood is returned per protocol. Before dialysis she was weighed in her school uniform, without shoes.
n4.prompt: How do you weigh her now?

choices.text: Weigh her on the same scale, in the same clothes and without shoes, and record it with the conditions.
choices.feedback: Only comparable weights tell you what was really removed and inform the target-weight review.

choices.text: Weigh her in her jacket and shoes, since she is leaving.
choices.feedback: Extra clothing makes the post-weight look higher and hides how much fluid was removed.
choices.then: You reweigh her under the pre-dialysis conditions.

choices.text: Skip the post-weight because she was unwell.
choices.feedback: She is well now. The post-weight is the measurement the team most needs after an episode.
choices.then: You weigh her under the pre-dialysis conditions.

n5.prompt: What goes into your handoff and record?

choices.text: A structured handoff: the episode with times, vital signs, steps and fluid given, removal achieved, post-weight, how she is now, and a flag for target-weight review.
choices.feedback: Structured handoffs were associated with fewer errors in pediatric hospitals. The flag turns one bad hour into a better plan for next time.
It hides the episode and the reason the target was missed. The next nurse may repeat the same plan.
choices.then: You rewrite it with the episode and the review flag.

choices.text: Tell her mother, in front of Jasmine, that she must have drunk too much again.
choices.feedback: There is no evidence for that, and blame in front of a child damages trust. Intolerance near target weight is common and may mean the target needs review.
choices.then: You apologize and give a factual handoff with the review flag.

end.title: Home, with a review booked
end.text: Jasmine leaves walking and chatting. The nephrologist will review her target weight and removal plan before the next session. You record the times, vital signs, steps, fluid given and removed, and her condition at discharge.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Behavior and heart rate come first. Yawning, quietness and a rising heart rate preceded any fall in blood pressure.
  • Act on the trend. Lay flat, reduce or pause removal per protocol, call.
  • Fluid by order, not by guess. The prescriber decides on fluid and on the rest of the session.
  • Do not chase the target. After an episode, a revised goal is safer, and the target weight may need review.
  • Comparable weights and an honest handoff turn the episode into a better plan.
